chapters.title: Chapter 2: How to Actually Buy and Sell Unlisted Shares in India

lessons.title: The Main Routes to Access Unlisted Shares: ESOPs, Placements and Dealer Platforms

children.text: Meena has decided she does want real exposure to unlisted companies, done properly this time. Her question shifts from "is this specific offer legitimate" to something more basic: what are the actual routes into an unlisted company's cap table for someone in her position, and which one actually fits a ₹15–20 lakh ticket size?

body.text: There are only a handful of real routes into an unlisted company's cap table. Everything else, a WhatsApp forward, a slick website, a friend-of-a-friend deal, is just a different sales pitch wrapped around one of these same few underlying routes.

children.text: Route 1: Buying Vested ESOP Shares From Employees

Startups grant Employee Stock Options (ESOPs) that vest over several years, giving employees the right to buy company shares later at a fixed price. Long before any IPO, some employees, especially early hires at well-funded companies during their growth years, want to convert part of that paper wealth into cash. A buyer can step in and purchase an employee's shares, once those options have actually been exercised into real shares, typically at ticket sizes far smaller than a company's own funding rounds, sometimes just a few lakh rupees for a handful of shares.
Route 2: Participating Directly in a Late-Stage Private Placement

A company can also issue you brand new shares directly, as part of a funding round, under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013, which governs private placements. This is the route venture funds and large institutional investors use. It is rarely open to individual retail investors, both because the company chooses who it invites into a round and because tickets typically start at ₹1 crore or more. If a dealer offers to get you into a company's "funding round" at a much smaller ticket size, you are almost certainly not actually being placed in the round itself, whatever the pitch implies.
Route 3: Buying From an Existing Shareholder via a Secondary Sale

This is the route most retail and HNI investors actually use, whether they realise it or not. An existing shareholder, an early angel investor, a departing employee, or another private investor looking for partial liquidity, sells some of their shares to a new buyer. Ticket sizes here can run from a few lakh rupees upward, and this is where dealer platforms and brokers mostly operate: not creating new shares, but connecting an existing holder who wants to sell with a new buyer who wants in.
Route 4: Pooled Vehicles — AIFs and PMS With Pre-IPO Allocations

markDefs.definition: A SEBI-registered pooled investment vehicle. Category II AIFs commonly run late-stage or pre-IPO strategies, with a regulatory minimum investment of ₹1 crore per investor.

Portfolio Management Services, where a SEBI-registered manager runs a portfolio on behalf of individual investors, sometimes including unlisted or pre-IPO allocations, subject to its own minimum investment and fee structure.

children.text: For investors who would rather not bet on a single unlisted company, or who do not have a large enough ticket for direct placement,
Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)
registered with SEBI, and some
Portfolio Management Services (PMS)

, run dedicated pre-IPO or late-stage strategies. You invest in the fund, and the fund's manager picks and holds a basket of unlisted companies on your behalf. This route brings real SEBI oversight of the fund manager, which none of the other three routes have, but it comes with a regulatory minimum investment, management and performance fees, and a fund lock-in of its own.

children.text: What Actually Determines the Price You Pay

Only one of these four routes has anything resembling independent price discovery, and even that is limited to the specific investors negotiating that specific round. A dealer quoting you a price for a secondary sale is not reading off an exchange. They are pricing off the company's last known funding round valuation, adjusted by whatever premium or discount their own inventory, and their sense of your appetite, suggests. Two dealers can quote meaningfully different prices for the same company's shares on the same day, and neither is more "official" than the other.

body.text: A dealer's quoted price is a starting point for negotiation, not a market price in the sense you are used to from NSE-listed shares. Always ask what the quote is benchmarked against, typically the last funding round, and how old that round actually is.

body.title: Matching the Route to Your Situation
steps: If your ticket size is under ₹5–10 lakh, a secondary purchase from an existing shareholder via a reputable dealer is usually your only realistic route
If you have ₹1 crore or more and want diversification rather than a single-company bet, an AIF or PMS with a pre-IPO mandate deserves a look
If you are being invited to participate directly in a funding round, confirm you are dealing with the company itself, not a dealer claiming to represent it
Whatever the route, insist on the same formal transfer steps covered in the previous lesson: signed SPA, Form SH-4, and demat credit
Treat any route promising retail-sized tickets (₹10,000–₹50,000) into a "pre-IPO" company with extra scepticism, since genuine access at that size is rare

children.text: ESOP Secondary Sales, in a Bit More Detail

markDefs.definition: The process by which an employee earns the right to exercise stock options over time, commonly across three to four years from the grant date.
Paying the company the pre-agreed exercise price to convert vested stock options into actual shares. Only exercised shares can typically be sold to an outside buyer.

children.text: An ESOP grant does not hand an employee shares directly. Options
vest
over a period, commonly three to four years, and once vested, an employee can choose to
exercise

them, paying the company a pre-agreed exercise price to actually convert options into real shares. Only shares that exist after this step can legally be sold to an outside buyer. "Vested options" that have not yet been exercised are, in most schemes, not transferable to anyone outside the company at all.

body.text: Many ESOP schemes also require the company's own approval, or give it a Right of First Refusal, before an employee can sell shares to someone outside the company, even after exercise. A seller who breezily promises to "transfer once you pay" may not have checked whether their own company will actually permit the transfer at all.

body.title: The "Fully Vested" ESOP Offer
body.scenario: An early employee at a startup offers to sell Meena their "fully vested ESOPs" directly, for cash, at ₹380 a share, promising to "transfer once you pay."
body.prompt: What should Meena confirm before paying, given everything covered in this lesson and the last one?
body.modelAnswer: "Vested" is not the same as "exercised", so Meena's first question should be whether these options have actually been exercised into real, existing shares. If not, there is nothing yet that can legally be sold to her. Next, she needs to check whether the company's own ESOP scheme even permits a sale to an outside buyer, since many schemes require company approval or give the company a Right of First Refusal specifically over ESOP shares. Finally, exactly as in the previous lesson, she should insist on a signed SPA, payment via a traceable banking channel directly to the seller, execution of Form SH-4, and independent confirmation through her own demat account once the deal is meant to be done, rather than accepting "transfer once you pay" as a plan.

body.title: What Actually Matters in an ESOP Offer
body.question: An early employee at a startup tells you they want to sell you their "vested ESOPs" directly, for cash, before any IPO. What is the most important thing to verify first?
options: That the exercise price they originally paid was reasonable
Whether the options have actually been exercised into shares, and whether the company's ESOP scheme even permits an external sale
That the startup is a well-known unicorn
That the employee has worked at the company for more than two years
body.explanation: Unexercised options generally cannot be sold directly to an outside buyer, and even after exercise, many ESOP schemes restrict or require company approval for a transfer to someone outside the company. Both must be checked before anything else matters.

body.title: From Option to Share
body.textWithBlank: Before an employee's stock options can be sold or transferred to an outside buyer, they must first be converted into actual shares through a step called ___.
body.explanation: Exercising means paying the pre-agreed exercise price to convert vested options into real, existing shares. Only exercised shares can typically be sold onward.

children.text: AIFs and PMS: The More Regulated Route

Because AIFs and PMS providers are themselves registered with and supervised by SEBI, this route brings a layer of regulatory oversight none of the other three have, even though the underlying unlisted companies they invest in remain just as unlisted and illiquid as ever. What an investor gets in return for the ₹1 crore minimum and the fees is diversification across several companies picked by a professional manager, rather than a concentrated bet on one, plus the comfort of dealing with a regulated entity instead of an individual dealer. What they give up is control over which specific companies they are exposed to, and liquidity: most such funds run for seven to ten years, sometimes longer with extensions, and an investor's money is genuinely locked in for that period.

children.text: Putting It Together

None of these four routes is inherently the "right" one. The one that fits depends on ticket size, whether an investor wants a single-company bet or diversified exposure, and how much illiquidity they can genuinely tolerate. What does not change across any of them is the discipline from the previous lesson: a signed agreement naming the real party on the other side, payment through traceable banking channels, the actual Companies Act paperwork, and a demat credit you can check yourself.

cards.definition: Employee Stock Option Plan: the right, granted to employees, to buy company shares later at a fixed exercise price, after a vesting period.
Paying the pre-agreed exercise price to convert vested stock options into actual, sellable shares.
A company issuing new shares directly to selected investors in a funding round, governed by Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013.
A SEBI-registered pooled investment vehicle. Category II AIFs commonly run late-stage or pre-IPO strategies, with a ₹1 crore regulatory minimum investment.
A SEBI-registered manager running an individual investor's portfolio, sometimes including unlisted or pre-IPO allocations.
A sale of already-issued shares by an existing shareholder to a new buyer, as opposed to the company issuing brand new shares.

points: There are four real routes into unlisted shares: buying vested, exercised ESOP shares from employees; direct participation in a company's private placement; buying from an existing shareholder in a secondary sale; and pooled AIF or PMS vehicles with a pre-IPO mandate.
Direct private placements and SEBI-registered AIFs both typically require a minimum ticket of ₹1 crore or more, putting them out of reach for most retail investors.
Most retail and HNI investors actually access unlisted shares through ESOP or existing-shareholder secondary sales, usually facilitated by a dealer or platform.
Unexercised stock options generally cannot be sold to an outside buyer, and even exercised ESOP shares are often restricted by the company's own approval rights or Right of First Refusal.

A dealer's quoted price is not an exchange price. It is typically benchmarked to the company's last funding round valuation, adjusted by the dealer's own view of demand, and can vary meaningfully between dealers.

Whichever route you use, the same formal-transfer discipline applies: a signed agreement naming the real seller, traceable payment, proper Companies Act paperwork, and an independently verified demat credit.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Meena is fictional and used purely for illustration, and the routes-by-share figures shown are illustrative estimates, not an official industry statistic. Minimum investment amounts and regulations cited, such as the ₹1 crore SEBI AIF threshold, should be independently verified against current SEBI regulations before acting, since regulatory minimums can change.
